To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the null/low-activities of GSTM1 and GSTP genes are significantly associated with increased risk of bladder cancer and that the risk of bladder cancer is further increased by the presence of the slow acetylation genotype of NAT2 in individuals with known high exposure to arylamines

null genotypes of GSTT1, GSTM1 and GSTP are associated with increased risk of bladder cancer, that slow NAT2 acetylator phenotype is associated with increased risk among high arylamine exposed subjects, and that the effects of NAT2 slow phenotype are modified by GST genotypes.
null/low- activity genotypes of GST genes are associated with an increased risk of bladder cancer and the effect is strongest among individuals with known exposures to carcinogenic aromatic amines.
In summary, our research is concerned with
genetic factors that may alter susceptibility to bladder cancer in relation to exposure to carcinogens in tobacco smoke.
the role of genetic factors in the metabolism of tobacco and other carcinogens in relation with the risk of bladder cancer.
the genetic determinants of the metabolism of carcinogens in relation with the risk of bladder cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of two null/low- activity GST genes, and NAT2 slow acetylators, are associated with increased risk of bladder cancer.

the presence of null/low activity GST genotypes is a risk factor for bladder cancer and that NAT2 slow acetylators are at increased risk of bladder cancer when they have high exposures to carcinogens.

null/low- activity genotypes of GST genes and slow acetylation genotype of NAT2 were associated with increased risk of bladder cancer, particularly in subjects with known high exposures of arylamines.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
individuals with two or more null or low-activity GST genotpyes have an increased risk of bladder cancer, especially those with slow NAT2 acetylation.

individuals with two or more low-activity GST genotypic variants and NAT2 slow acetylators have a 4.2 times increased risk of bladder cancer compared to those without these variants (P for interaction = 0.0001).

the null genotypes of GST genes are associated with a moderate increase in the risk of bladder cancer and that slow acetylation of NAT2 may increase risk among individuals with high exposures to arylamines.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the null/low-activities of GSTM1 and GSTP are associated with an increased risk of bladder cancer, and that the null/ low-activity genotypes are associated in a monotonic manner with risk.
genetic variation in GST genes may be a significant risk factor for bladder cancer, especially among individuals with occupational exposure to arylamines.

the combined effect of genetic polymorphisms in GSTM1, -T1 and -P1 on bladder cancer risk is greater than the effect of any one gene, and the effect of the GST polymorphisms is stronger among those with known high exposures.
